text.p: These are the leading stories in the Kenyan press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Kenyan government admits that the 11-year-old 8-4-4 system of education, with eight years in primary school, four at secondary level and four at university, is expensive and requires a lot of physical facilities and equipment.
- General Mahmoud Mohammed to hand top military job of chief of general staff to the long-serving and highly experienced General Daudi Tonje, a member of President Daniel arap Moi's small Tugen clan.
- Electoral Commission chairman Justice Zacchaeus Chesoni creates 22 new constituencies, raising the number of contestable parliamentary seats to 210.
- Opposition politician Mwai Kibaki and farmer/politician Njenga Karume tell milk firm Kenya Cooperative Creameries to seek a court order to end government interference in its affairs.

- Kenyans react with anger and sympathy to revelations by directors of supermarket chain Nakumatt Holdings Ltd that they received anonymous threats warning them to pay 50 million shillings "protection money" or face being closed down.
- The 1996 world investment report reveals that Foreign Direct Investments flow into Kenya has declined at an alarming rate despite positive change in the country's trade and investment regime.
- The recently-formed opposition national alliance comes under attack for hijacking matters of national concern to gain cheap publicity.

- Trade unionists appeal to the government to involve their members in the running of pension revenue schemes in the government and private sectors, including the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) for the benefit of workers.
